body:
How digestion and nutrition are connected

A balanced diet supplies nutrients, but the body must also digest food and absorb its useful components. Digestive illness can interfere with these processes. It may reduce appetite, disturb normal bowel function or cause the loss of water and salts.

Digestive disorders and deficiency diseases are not the same. A deficiency disease results from inadequate availability of a nutrient over time. A digestive disorder may be caused by infection, altered bowel movement or other conditions, although some digestive illnesses can eventually contribute to nutritional deficiency.

Diarrhoea: loss of water and salts

Diarrhoea generally means passing 3 or more loose or liquid stools in a day, or passing loose stools more frequently than is normal for the individual. It is often caused by an intestinal infection spread through contaminated food or water, though other causes are possible.

During diarrhoea, the body loses water and electrolytes, which are dissolved salts important for normal body functions. Severe fluid loss can cause dehydration. Young children are particularly vulnerable.

Role of oral rehydration solution

Oral rehydration solution (ORS) contains glucose and essential salts in water. It helps the intestine absorb water and replace fluids and electrolytes lost during diarrhoea. Properly prepared packaged ORS using safe water is an important treatment for dehydration caused by diarrhoea.

ORS does not directly kill the microorganisms that may cause the illness. Its main purpose is to prevent or correct dehydration. Safe drinking water, handwashing, sanitation and hygienic food preparation reduce the risk of many diarrhoeal infections.

Nutritious feeding, including breastfeeding where applicable, should generally continue during diarrhoeal illness. Blood in the stool, persistent diarrhoea, inability to drink, marked lethargy or signs of severe dehydration require prompt medical care.

Constipation: difficulty passing stools

Constipation commonly involves hard stools, difficulty passing stools or bowel movements that are less frequent than usual. It can be associated with inadequate dietary fibre, insufficient fluid intake or reduced physical activity, although medicines and medical conditions can also contribute.

Fibre helps form stools and maintain normal bowel movement. Drinking adequate water supports normal bowel function. Whole grains, pulses, fruits and vegetables are useful fibre sources.

Constipation is not a named vitamin-deficiency disease. Increasing fibre may help many people, but persistent or severe constipation can require medical evaluation.

Indigestion and related discomfort

Indigestion is a general term for discomfort in the upper abdomen, often involving fullness, bloating, nausea or discomfort after eating. It may be associated with eating habits or digestive conditions. It should not automatically be attributed to lack of a particular vitamin or mineral.

Overeating or eating foods that repeatedly provoke symptoms may worsen discomfort in some people. Persistent, severe or recurrent symptoms require medical assessment rather than assuming a simple dietary cause.

Comparing the conditions

ConditionMain problemNutrition connection
DiarrhoeaFrequent loose or liquid stoolsLoss of water and salts; repeated illness may worsen nutrition
ConstipationHard or difficult stoolsMay be associated with low fibre or inadequate fluids
IndigestionUpper abdominal discomfort after eatingMay affect eating; not itself a specific nutrient deficiency

Remember: Fibre helps normal passage of stools. ORS replaces water and electrolytes lost in diarrhoea. Neither fibre nor ORS can be treated as a replacement for all essential nutrients.

Prelims focus

  • Diarrhoea involves frequent loose or liquid stools and may cause dehydration.
  • ORS contains glucose and salts and helps replace lost water and electrolytes.
  • ORS is a rehydration treatment, not an antibiotic.
  • Dietary fibre supports normal bowel movements.
  • Low fibre and inadequate fluid intake can contribute to constipation.
  • Trap: Indigestion, diarrhoea and constipation are not interchangeable names for nutrient-deficiency diseases.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Ch. 2, Nutrition in Animals, printed pp. 16–18, including the section on diarrhoea; NCERT, Biology, Class 11, Ch. Digestion and Absorption, section on disorders of the digestive system; World Health Organization, Diarrhoeal Disease, 7 March 2024, sections Overview, Dehydration and Prevention and Treatment, consulted 3 November 2026; GCERT, Standard 6 Science (Curiosity), Ch. 3, printed pp. 46–47, on dietary fibre and water.]

title: Common Digestive Problems and Their Nutritional Effects

body:
Why are public nutrition measures needed?

Individual food choices are important, but nutritional problems can also arise when families have limited access to diverse foods, safe water or healthcare. Public nutrition measures therefore support dietary improvement, maternal and child nutrition, micronutrient deficiency prevention and the identification of undernutrition.

For this topic, the main distinction is between improving food intake, adding missing nutrients to foods and providing targeted nutrition or health services. These approaches complement one another.

Food fortification

Fortification means adding one or more nutrients to a food to improve its nutritional quality. Iodised salt is a familiar example because iodine is added to salt to help prevent iodine-deficiency disorders.

Double-fortified salt contains added iodine and iron. Fortification is useful when an essential nutrient may otherwise be insufficient in the diet, but fortified foods do not replace the need for a varied balanced diet.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is the national food regulator responsible for food safety and standards, including standards relevant to food fortification.

Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0

The Government of India's Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0 brings together nutrition-related services, including Anganwadi Services, POSHAN Abhiyaan and the Scheme for Adolescent Girls.

Through Anganwadi Services, supplementary nutrition is provided to eligible children from 6 months to 6 years, pregnant women and lactating mothers. Other services include early childhood education, nutrition and health education, immunisation, health check-ups and referral services. Immunisation, health check-ups and referrals are delivered in coordination with the National Health Mission and public health services.

POSHAN Abhiyaan was launched on 8 March 2018. It promotes improved nutritional outcomes through coordination among departments, community participation, awareness and improved nutrition practices. The older Integrated Child Development Services programme, commonly called ICDS, was launched in 1975 and its Anganwadi Services were subsequently reorganised under Mission POSHAN 2.0.

Anaemia Mukt Bharat

Anaemia Mukt Bharat, continued as Anemia Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan under the revised 2026 guidelines, is a national strategy to reduce anaemia among children, adolescents and women through a life-cycle approach. Its measures include iron and folic acid supplementation, deworming, nutrition awareness, testing and treatment of anaemia, and attention to non-nutritional causes.

This programme illustrates why anaemia prevention cannot be limited to telling people to eat more iron-rich foods. Anaemia may have nutritional and non-nutritional causes, so a combination of dietary support and appropriate healthcare is needed.

PM POSHAN and school nutrition

PM POSHAN, or Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman, is the school-meal programme associated with nutritious cooked meals for eligible children in government and government-aided schools. Its educational and nutritional purpose is to support children through regular school meals.

The Ministry of Education's published programme-approval information records an approved scheme period from 2021–22 to 2025–26, followed by an interim extension up to 30 September 2026 or earlier approval for the next cycle. As of the content cutoff of 3 November 2026, that cited approval page does not establish a later final approval. The programme's name and purpose should therefore be distinguished from any unverified claim about its subsequent funding approval.

Gujarat's Poshan Sudha scheme

Poshan Sudha is a Gujarat government nutrition initiative focused on pregnant and lactating women, particularly in tribal areas. According to the Gujarat Women and Child Development Department's information published on 31 January 2023, the scheme began as a pilot in 2017–18 in 10 blocks of 5 districts: Dahod, Valsad, Mahisagar, Chhota Udepur and Narmada.

That published account records approval for expansion from 2022–23 to 14 tribal districts and 106 blocks. The reported benefits include a full meal for registered pregnant and lactating women at Anganwadi centres, along with iron and calcium tablets and nutrition education.

These district and block figures describe the expansion reported in the department's 2023 publication. They should not automatically be treated as a newly verified count for November 2026.

How the programmes differ

Measure or programmeMain focusKey distinction
Iodised salt and food fortificationMicronutrient improvementNutrients are added to food
Mission POSHAN 2.0Maternal, child and eligible adolescent nutritionIntegrated Anganwadi and nutrition services
Anaemia Mukt BharatAnaemia prevention and reductionSupplementation, screening and other interventions
PM POSHANSchool nutritionCooked meals for eligible schoolchildren
Poshan Sudha, GujaratPregnant and lactating womenMeal and nutrition support through Anganwadi centres in covered areas

Connecting the whole lesson

The essential nutritional relationships can be revised together. Carbohydrates and fats mainly provide energy; proteins support growth and repair; vitamins and minerals are necessary for normal body functions. Vitamin A deficiency is associated with night blindness, B1 with beriberi, C with scurvy and D with rickets. Iron deficiency can cause anaemia, while iodine deficiency can cause goitre.

Digestion breaks down complex food, and absorption makes nutrients available to the body. A balanced diet provides the needed nutrients in appropriate quantities along with fibre and water. Food fortification and public nutrition programmes support this goal, but neither replaces dietary diversity or appropriate medical care.

Prelims focus

  • Fortification adds nutrients to food; iodised salt is a familiar example.
  • POSHAN Abhiyaan was launched on 8 March 2018; ICDS began in 1975.
  • Mission POSHAN 2.0 integrates Anganwadi and related nutrition services.
  • Anaemia Mukt Bharat addresses anaemia through nutritional and healthcare interventions.
  • Gujarat's Poshan Sudha began as a pilot in 2017–18, according to the state department's published account.
  • Trap: Nutrition programmes have different target groups; PM POSHAN school meals and Gujarat's Poshan Sudha maternal nutrition support are not the same programme.

[Sources: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, Fortified Food guidance, consulted 3 November 2026; Ministry of Women and Child Development, Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, Brief and FAQs, consulted 3 November 2026; National Health Mission, Anaemia Mukt Bharat, programme overview and operational guidelines, consulted 3 November 2026; Ministry of Education, PM POSHAN Programme Approval Board Meetings, scheme-approval period and interim-extension information, consulted 3 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Women and Child Development Department, Poshan Sudha, published 31 January 2023, consulted 3 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 6, Ch. 2, Components of Food, printed pp. 12–16; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Ch. 2, Nutrition in Animals, printed pp. 11–20.]
